title: Micah 1:1–9
context: The book opens with “The LORD’s word that came to Micah of Morasheth” in the days of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, concerning Samaria and Jerusalem (1:1). The prophet summons the peoples to hear as the LORD comes down in judgment (1:2–4). The LORD names Samaria and Jerusalem as the centers of Jacob’s sin and announces Samaria’s ruin (1:5–7), and Micah laments that the wound has reached Judah and the gate of Jerusalem (1:8–9). Shared ground: the LORD judges his own people for real sin, and his prophet grieves as he speaks.

verses.text: The LORD’s word that came to Micah of Morasheth in the days of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah, which he saw concerning Samaria and Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes: The heading names “Micah of Morasheth” and dates his ministry to the days of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah. Arminian readers see a prophet addressing real kings and cities, calling a particular generation to repentance.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the word of the LORD given in history, concerning both Samaria and Jerusalem. Shared ground: the prophecy is received as the LORD’s word, not Micah’s own opinion, and it speaks to both kingdoms.

verses.text: Hear, you peoples, all of you! Listen, O earth, and all that is therein. Let the Lord GOD be witness against you, the Lord from his holy temple.
verses.arminianNotes: “Hear, you peoples, all of you! Listen, O earth.” Arminian readers see the LORD calling the nations to witness his case against his people, as in a court where all may hear.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear a courtroom summons with the Lord GOD as witness “from his holy temple.” Shared ground: the God of Israel is Lord of all peoples, and his judgment of his own people is public and just.

verses.text: For behold, the LORD comes out of his place, and will come down and tread on the high places of the earth.
verses.arminianNotes: “For behold, the LORD comes out of his place, and will come down and tread on the high places of the earth.” Arminian readers see the LORD coming in judgment, his majesty overturning every human height.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a theophany of judgment. The “high places” can mean both mountain heights and places of false worship, and readers in this tradition hear both senses in the word.

verses.text: The mountains melt under him, and the valleys split apart like wax before the fire, like waters that are poured down a steep place.
verses.arminianNotes: “The mountains melt under him, and the valleys split apart like wax before the fire.” Arminian readers see poetic images of creation trembling before its Maker as he comes to judge.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see figurative language for the overwhelming presence of God. Shared ground: such imagery, found also in the Psalms, expresses the LORD’s holiness and power rather than a literal geological forecast.

verses.text: “All this is for the disobedience of Jacob, and for the sins of the house of Israel. What is the disobedience of Jacob? Isn’t it Samaria? And what are the high places of Judah? Aren’t they Jerusalem?
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says, “All this is for the disobedience of Jacob.” Arminian readers see the capitals themselves, Samaria and Jerusalem, named as the centers of the nation’s sin and therefore of its judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the leading cities held responsible. Shared ground: the sins of the powerful shape a whole people, and judgment begins where privilege and responsibility are greatest.

verses.text: Therefore I will make Samaria like a rubble heap of the field, like places for planting vineyards; and I will pour down its stones into the valley, and I will uncover its foundations.
verses.arminianNotes: “Therefore I will make Samaria like a rubble heap of the field.” Arminian readers see the northern capital reduced to farmland, a sober picture of judgment on a proud city.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD’s sentence on Samaria. Many readers connect the oracle with the city’s fall to Assyria, though readers in this tradition hold precise dating with care.

verses.text: All her idols will be beaten to pieces, all her temple gifts will be burned with fire, and I will destroy all her images; for of the hire of a prostitute has she gathered them, and to the hire of a prostitute shall they return.”
verses.arminianNotes: “All her idols will be beaten to pieces.” The LORD describes Samaria’s images as gathered from the hire of a prostitute. Arminian readers see idolatry pictured as unfaithfulness to the covenant God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the image of spiritual unfaithfulness, read soberly. Shared ground: wealth gained through false worship will be lost the same way, and idols cannot protect those who trust them.

verses.text: For this I will lament and wail. I will go stripped and naked. I will howl like the jackals and mourn like the ostriches.
verses.arminianNotes: “For this I will lament and wail. I will go stripped and naked.” Arminian readers see the prophet grieving over the judgment he announces, not delighting in it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see Micah’s lament as a sign of compassion. Readers in this tradition note that a faithful messenger feels the weight of the word he brings, as other prophets also did.

verses.text: For her wounds are incurable; for it has come even to Judah. It reaches to the gate of my people, even to Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes: “For her wounds are incurable; for it has come even to Judah. It reaches to the gate of my people, even to Jerusalem.” Arminian readers see judgment spreading from Samaria to Judah’s capital.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the threat reaching Jerusalem. Shared ground: Judah is warned by Samaria’s fate, and the prophet’s grief deepens as the danger comes closer to his own people.
